notes: \cpara{Picks up from ``Quantum Explanations'' two days earlier and asks what the world is made of, if not particles or waves.}
\cpara{Describes the first set-up: a half-silvered mirror at A and two detectors. I could not view the figures; my notes follow the text's descriptions of them.}
\cpara{Reports the observation correctly: with a half-silvered mirror, each photon is detected at one detector, about half the time at each.}
\cpara{Gives the ``early scientists''' reading of that result: the mirror reflects the photon half the time. The scientists are not named.}

\cpara{Mocks the reading before giving any evidence against it. For Figure 1 alone, the reading that the mirror deflects the photon half the time predicts exactly what is observed; the post shows where it fails only with Figure 2. The mockery is the method announced in ``Quantum Explanations.''}
\cpara{Introduces the post's device: a program that is the experiment, not one that predicts it. This puts the realism declared in the previous post into a picture.}
\cpara{Defines a configuration, here ``a photon heading toward A.''}
\cpara{Gives the configuration a complex value, $-1$. The choice is free, as the post says (``The exact value doesn't matter so long as it's not zero''), since only ratios will be observed.}
\cpara{Asserts that configurations and their values are in the territory, not in anyone's knowledge. The argument for this comes at the end of the post.}
\cpara{Names the complex values amplitudes, and notes that they cannot be probabilities, since probabilities are real numbers between 0 and 1. That is correct.}
\cpara{Adds the two outgoing configurations.}

\cpara{Gives the rule, flagged ``Roughly speaking'': multiply by 1 going straight, by $i$ when turned. This is the standard ``symmetric'' beam splitter (Wikipedia, ``Beam splitter,'' citing Loudon), except that there both factors are also divided by $\sqrt{2}$. Without that factor the total of the squared moduli is not kept at 1: in Figure 2 it is 1 before A, 2 after A and 4 after D. The post compares only configurations that have passed the same number of half-mirrors, so every result it reports comes out right.}
\cpara{Applies the rule. The arithmetic is right: $(-1)\times i = -i$ and $(-1)\times 1 = -1$.}
\cpara{Notes, correctly, that travel adds a complex factor that depends on distance, and sets it to 1 for simplicity.}
\cpara{Lists the final state. The values match the computation above.}
\cpara{Stresses that the amplitudes come out the same on every run. What differs between runs, which detector clicks, the post leaves for later.}
\cpara{Says amplitudes cannot be read off directly, and puts the reason at a ``higher level of organization.''}

\cpara{Introduces the squared modulus, $a^2 + b^2$ (printed here as ``(a2+b2)''), with the picture of an arrow in the plane. Feynman used the same picture for a general audience in \textsc{QED} (1985): ``All we do is draw little arrows on a piece of paper'' (as quoted on Wikiquote).}
\cpara{Refines the claim: only ratios of squared moduli are observed. This is what lets the post leave out the factor $1/\sqrt{2}$ noted above.}
\cpara{Reports that the two detectors' configurations have equal squared moduli, and promises that further experiments fix the ratio of the amplitudes.}

\clogic{Loosely worded. An interferometer shows only the total phase difference between two paths, mirrors and distances together. The editor's note at the end gives a different rule, $-1$ for a turn, which also makes one detector dark; so the experiments shown do not single out $i$.}

\cpara{Identifies the tool: counts of detector clicks are in the ratio of the squared moduli. This is the Born rule, whose reason the post says it will not ``consider yet.'' Later in the book, ``Many Worlds, One Best Guess'' says: ``There is no known reason for the Born probabilities.''}
\cpara{Restates the one fact the tool gives for Figure 1: equal squared moduli.}
\cpara{Raises the obvious objection: for Figure 1, why not say the mirror reflects the photon half the time?}
\cpara{The first answer restates the view (``That's not how reality works''). The evidence comes with the next experiment.}
\cpara{Describes the second set-up: two half-mirrors and two full mirrors. It is a Mach--Zehnder interferometer, as the editor's note at the end says.}
\cpara{Sets the full-mirror factor to $i$ as well. Each path meets one full mirror, so whatever factor a real mirror gives cancels out of every result.}
\cpara{Explains why the two arrivals at D are separate configurations: they come from different directions, and the mirror treats them differently.}
\cpara{Restates the mirror rule.}
\cpara{The totals. The arithmetic is right: at E, $i + (-i) = 0$; at F, $1 + 1 = 2$ (recomputed in a short script).}
\cpara{Draws the observable result: no photon reaches E. This is the standard Mach--Zehnder result. With the factor $1/\sqrt{2}$ the amplitudes are 0 and 1, and every photon reaches F.}
\cpara{States the lesson: the result requires amplitude flows.}
\cpara{Works out the rival prediction. A ball deflected at random at each half-mirror would reach each detector half the time. That is correct.}
\cpara{Raises a second rival: each mirror marks the photon so that it takes the other turn at the next one.}
\cpara{Answers first with Occam's razor, then, in the next paragraph, with an experiment. The experiment is what settles it.}
\cpara{Describes the third set-up: a block between B and D.}
\cpara{The arithmetic is right: E receives $-i$ and F receives 1.}
\cpara{Draws the prediction: blocking one path lights the dark detector again. This is the standard result.}

\cfact{True of the photons that reach a detector. Half of all photons now stop at the block, and each detector fires for a quarter of those sent. The post's rule without the factor $1/\sqrt{2}$ would give the block a third instead (squared moduli 1, 1 and 1).}
\cpara{The arithmetic checks: with the other path blocked, E receives $i$ and F receives 1, and the ratio is again 1.}

\cpara{Correct for a particle that simply goes one way or the other under fixed rules: no such rule gives a dark detector in Figure 2 and a lit one in Figure 3. It does not cover pilot-wave theory, in which a particle takes one path but is guided by a wave that takes both. For a particle in a two-slit apparatus, ``the slit through which it passes and its location upon arrival on the photographic plate are completely determined by its initial position and wave function'' (Stanford Encyclopedia, ``Bohmian Mechanics''). That theory needs the amplitudes too, and the same entry calls it ``empirically equivalent to orthodox quantum theory.''}
\cpara{Names the mechanism: amplitudes from two configurations can cancel. This is the center of the post, and it is correct.}

\cpara{Argues that probabilities cannot cancel, because none is negative. The fractions printed here as ``12,'' ``13'' and ``16'' are $1/2$, $1/3$ and $1/6$, and the arithmetic is right: $1/2 \times 1/3 = 1/6$.}
\cpara{Adds the author's view, from ``Probability is in the Mind,'' that probabilities describe states of knowledge, while amplitudes are in the territory.}
\cpara{Concludes that configurations are not propositions or possible worlds: they are ``simply real.''}
\cpara{Warns against the phrasing on which the path not taken ``interferes'' with the photon.}
\cpara{Argues, with a car that nearly hits you, that only real events have effects: what affects you is your real act of imagining, not the accident that did not happen.}
\cpara{Says that crediting the accident that did not happen with a causal effect confuses map and territory.}

\cpara{The argument for realism, in one step: amplitudes have visible effects, so they are real. Later work supports the post against one kind of rival. Pusey, Barrett and Rudolph (2012) showed that, under a ``seemingly natural independence assumption,'' the quantum state cannot be mere knowledge about an underlying physical state. The Stanford Encyclopedia adds that the theorem ``does not close off all options for anti-realism about quantum states.''}

\clogic{Correct as stated. It does not reach epistemic views such as QBism, which do not say that amplitudes are degrees of belief. On QBism, a quantum state ``represents the epistemic state of the one who assigns it'' by ``specifying the agent's coherent degree of belief (credence)'' in the outcomes of possible measurements (Stanford Encyclopedia, ``Quantum-Bayesian and Pragmatist Views'').}
\cpara{Grants that the post's configurations were simplified: real ones involve many particles, and the next post will show this.}
\cpara{Says that each configuration should have included the particles of the mirrors and detectors.}

\clogic{This is the picture of quantum mechanics with a fixed number of particles. The post's own photons belong to quantum field theory, where the electromagnetic field is, in the Stanford Encyclopedia's words, ``impossible to deal with in the frame of QM,'' and where ``the lack of position operators'' troubles a particle reading. The sequence does not discuss field theory.}
\cpara{Grants that the post's discrete configurations were a simplification of a continuous space.}

\cpara{The note is the book editors'. Both rules are in standard sources. The $-1$ rule is for a dielectric coating; Wikipedia's ``Beam splitter'' says it ``does not apply to partial reflection by conductive (metallic) coatings,'' which is what half-silvered'' literally describes. The post's $i$ rule is Loudon's ``symmetric'' beam splitter, given in the same article. Either rule gives a dark detector in Figure 2; with $-1$, which detector is dark depends on which side of D is coated.}
